lessons.title: શું …? (śũ …?) — the yes-or-no question
lessons.gloss: the śũ you know as what, moved to the front, where it asks for yes or no

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say શું, what, as in your name: તમારું નામ શું છે. Then the two oldest answers in the book, હા and ના. And one sentence from the last chapter: I don't speak Gujarati.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: શું at the front

segments.text: શું તમે ગુજરાતી બોલો છો? — śũ tame gujarātī bolo cho? — Do you speak Gujarati?

Inside a sentence શું means what. At the very front it means nothing at all: it marks the sentence as a yes-or-no question, and not one other word moves. English rebuilds the sentence around do; Gujarati sets a flag at the front.
તમારું નામ શું છે — what is your name — inside;
શું તમે ગુજરાતી બોલો છો — do you speak Gujarati — in front.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the voice can carry it

segments.text: In speech the flag often drops, and the voice does its work: તમે ગુજરાતી બોલો છો? with the pitch rising on the last word asks the same question. On the page the question mark carries the rise.
Gujarati answers with હા or ના, and then, usually, with the verb again:
હા, હું ગુજરાતી બોલું છું. — hā, hũ gujarātī bolũ chũ. ના, હું ગુજરાતી નથી બોલતો. — nā, hũ gujarātī nathī bolto.

lessons.title: કે નહીં? and ખરું? — two tags at the end
lessons.gloss: or not, and right: two tags that close a yes-or-no question

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Ask do you speak Gujarati? twice: once with શું, once with your voice alone. Then say નહીં, the not for one word, and સાચું, true.
તમે આવો છો કે નહીં? — tame āvo cho ke nahī̃? — Are you coming or not?
The કે you know as that also means or between two choices. The tag offers both answers and asks the listener to pick one. It is firmer than શું: a parent at the door, a friend whose bus is leaving.
ખરું (kharũ) means true, real, a close neighbour of સાચું. As a tag it asks for agreement:
તમે અહીં રહો છો, ખરું? — tame ahī̃ raho cho, kharũ? — You live here, right?
The speaker already expects હા and checks it. So the three sound different: શું in front opens the question, કે નહીં at the end asks for a pick, and ખરું at the end asks for a yes.

lessons.title: મને, તને, તેને — the pronouns things happen to
lessons.gloss: to me, to you, to him or her: the pronouns that likes and fevers happen to

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Ask are you coming or not?, then you live here, right? And from the verb chapters long ago: મને ગુજરાતી ગમે છે, I like Gujarati.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the person something happens to

segments.text: In મને ગુજરાતી ગમે છે the thing liked is the subject, and I stand to one side as મને, to me. Gujarati speaks of a fever the same way: it arrives to someone.
મને તાવ છે. — mane tāv che. — I have a fever.
The to forms for one person:

utterances: who: I. pronoun: હું. to form: મને.
who: you (familiar). pronoun: તું. to form: તને.
who: he, she. pronoun: તે. to form: તેને.

segments.text: તમને has been in the book since the second day, inside તમને મળીને આનંદ થયો: to you, meeting, joy happened. Its partners:

utterances: who: we. pronoun: અમે. to form: અમને.
who: you (respectful). pronoun: તમે. to form: તમને.
who: they. pronoun: તેઓ. to form: તેમને.

segments.text: તેઓ turns into તેમ- before the ending: તેમને, to them.

lessons.title: મારો ભાઈ, મારી બહેન — my agrees with what is owned
lessons.gloss: my, agreeing with the thing owned and not with the owner

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say I have a fever and they like Gujarati. Then the first possessive you ever learned: મારું નામ, my name.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the ending follows the thing

segments.text: મારું ends in -ું because નામ is a neuter noun. Change the noun and my changes its last sign to match it:
મારો ભાઈ — māro bhāī — my brother: masculine, -ો;
મારી બહેન — mārī bahen — my sister: feminine, -ી;
મારું ઘર — mārũ ghar — my home: neuter, -ું;
મારા પિતા — mārā pitā — my father: -ા, for more than one, or for one person spoken of with respect.
A woman and a man say મારો ભાઈ alike. The ending follows the brother, not whoever owns him.

utterances: owner: હું. my, your, his: the -ું form: મારું.
owner: તું. my, your, his: the -ું form: તારું.

segments.text: તેનું નામ મીરા છે. — tenũ nām mīrā che. — Her name is Mira.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: more than one owner

segments.text: તેમનું comes from the same તેમ- as તેમને. Every one of them bends exactly as મારું does, to -ો, -ી, -ું or -ા:
તમારો ફોન — tamāro phon — your phone;
તેની બહેન — tenī bahen — his sister, or her sister;
આપણું ગામ — āpṇũ gām — our village, yours and mine;
તમારા પિતા, તેના પિતા — tamārā pitā, tenā pitā — your father, his or her father: respect takes -ા.
